API Design: Supporting Forward and Reverse Mode AD

Design Challenge

Forward-mode AD (ForwardDiff):

  • Works by propagating Dual numbers through computations
  • Efficient for few outputs, many inputs (e.g., Jacobians)
  • Requires explicit control over when Dual numbers are introduced
  • Benefits from manual composition of operations

Reverse-mode AD (Zygote/Enzyme):

  • Works by recording computation graph and backpropagating
  • Efficient for many outputs, few inputs (e.g., gradients of scalar loss)
  • Requires pure functions (no mutation)
  • Needs rrule definitions for custom operations

The Tension:

  • Forward-mode wants: scatter_parameters!(psys, p_dual) (mutation)
  • Reverse-mode wants: y = f(p) (pure function with rrule)

Recommended Design: Dual-Level API

Principle: Separate concerns by use case, not by AD backend

Low-level API (Explicit)     →  For forward-mode, manual control, debugging
High-level API (Declarative) →  For reverse-mode, optimization, composition

Both APIs use the same underlying primitives!

Low-Level API (Explicit Operations)

Purpose: Direct control, forward-mode AD, inspecting intermediate values

API:

# 1. Create system
psys = ParameterizedSystem(sys)
add_parameter!(psys, :PV, :pg, 1:100)
finalize_parameters!(psys)

# 2. Manually scatter parameters
p = gather_parameters(psys)
scatter_parameters!(psys, p)  # Can use Dual numbers here!

# 3. Manually solve
dae = DAE(Float64, sys)
ws = SystemResidualWorkspace(Float64, sys)
prob = NonlinearProblem(
    (g, y, _) -> begin
        copyto!(dae.y, y)
        evaluate_system_residuals!(ws, dae)
        copyto!(g, dae.g)
    end,
    dae.y
)
result = solve(prob, NewtonRaphson())
y = result.zero

# 4. Extract quantities
v = get_bus_voltages(sys, y)

Use cases:

  • Computing Jacobians (parameter_jacobian!, jacobian_sparsity_pattern)
  • Debugging
  • Custom AD workflows
  • Performance-critical code where you want explicit control

Example - Parameter Jacobian:

# This is forward-mode friendly
for param_idx in 1:n_params
    p_dual[param_idx] = Dual(p[param_idx], 1.0)
    scatter_parameters!(psys, p_dual)  # Scatter Dual numbers
    evaluate_system_residuals!(ws, dae)
    # Extract derivatives...
end

High-Level API (Pure Functions)

Purpose: Optimization, reverse-mode AD, composition with other packages

API:

# 1. Create system (same)
psys = ParameterizedSystem(sys)
add_parameter!(psys, :PV, :pg, 1:100)
finalize_parameters!(psys)

# 2. Pure function: p → y
y = solve_power_flow(psys, p; solver_opts...)

# 3. Compose with loss
function objective(p)
    y = solve_power_flow(psys, p)
    v = get_bus_voltages(psys.sys, y)
    return sum((v .- 1.0).^2)
end

# 4. Differentiate with ANY AD backend
using ForwardDiff
grad_fwd = ForwardDiff.gradient(objective, p)

using Zygote
grad_rev = Zygote.gradient(objective, p)

# Both work! Same API!

Key insight: solve_power_flow is a pure function with:

  • Clear input/output contract
  • No side effects (internally creates temp workspace)
  • rrule for reverse-mode efficiency

Implementation:

"""
    solve_power_flow(psys::ParameterizedSystem, p::AbstractVector; kwargs...)

Solve power flow equations with given parameters.

Pure function: No side effects, deterministic output.

# Returns
- `y::Vector`: Solution vector (algebraic variables)

# AD Support
- Forward-mode: Accepts `Vector{Dual}`, returns `Vector{Dual}`
- Reverse-mode: Has `rrule` for efficient implicit differentiation

# Example

julia

Works with any AD backend

using ForwardDiff y = solvepowerflow(psys, p) Jparam = ForwardDiff.jacobian(p -> solvepower_flow(psys, p), p)

using Zygote loss(p) = sum(solvepowerflow(psys, p).^2) grad = Zygote.gradient(loss, p)

"""
function solve_power_flow(
    psys::ParameterizedSystem,
    p::AbstractVector;
    solver=NewtonRaphson(),
    ftol=1e-8,
    maxiter=50
)
    # Scatter parameters (internal mutation is OK)
    scatter_parameters!(psys, p)

    # Create workspace (accepts Dual numbers via type inference)
    T = eltype(p)
    sys = psys.sys
    dae = DAE(T, sys)
    ws = SystemResidualWorkspace(T, sys)

    # Solve (works for both Float64 and Dual)
    prob = NonlinearProblem(
        (g, y, _) -> begin
            copyto!(dae.y, y)
            evaluate_system_residuals!(ws, dae)
            copyto!(g, dae.g)
        end,
        dae.y
    )
    result = solve(prob, NewtonRaphson(); abstol=ftol, maxiters=maxiter)

    if !SciMLBase.successful_retcode(result.retcode)
        @warn "Power flow did not converge" result
    end

    return result.u
end

ChainRules Integration (Reverse-Mode Efficiency)

using ChainRulesCore

function ChainRulesCore.rrule(
    ::typeof(solve_power_flow),
    psys::ParameterizedSystem,
    p::AbstractVector;
    cache=nothing,
    kwargs...
)
    # Forward pass (same as regular call)
    y = solve_power_flow(psys, p; kwargs...)

    # Prepare for reverse pass
    if isnothing(cache)
        cache = CachedAutodiffWorkspace(psys.sys)
    end

    function solve_power_flow_pullback(ȳ)
        # ȳ = ∂loss/∂y (from downstream)

        # Step 1: Compute J = ∂g/∂y at solution
        sparsity_y = jacobian_sparsity_pattern(psys.sys)
        colors_y = matrix_colors(sparsity_y)
        J = Float64.(sparsity_y)
        forwarddiff_color_jacobian!(J, cache, y; colorvec=colors_y)

        # Step 2: Solve adjoint: J^T λ = ȳ
        λ = J' \ ȳ

        # Step 3: Compute B = ∂g/∂p (use cached sparsity)
        if isnothing(psys.sparsity_dgdp)
            parameter_sparsity_pattern!(psys, cache)
        end
        B = Float64.(psys.sparsity_dgdp)
        compute_parameter_jacobian!(B, psys, cache, y, p)

        # Step 4: Chain rule: ∂loss/∂p = -λ^T · B
        p̄ = -B' * λ

        return (NoTangent(), NoTangent(), p̄)
    end

    return y, solve_power_flow_pullback
end

Key property: Users don't need to know rrule exists! It's automatically used by Zygote.

Comparison: When to Use Each API

AspectLow-Level APIHigh-Level API
ControlFull control over operationsAbstracted
PerformanceManually optimizedAutomatic (via rrule)
Use caseJacobians, debuggingOptimization, ML
AD modeForward-mode (explicit)Both (automatic)
MutationAllowed (scatter!)Hidden (pure function)
ComposabilityManualAutomatic
Learning curveSteeperGentle

Decision tree:

Need to compute parameter Jacobian?
├─ Yes → Use low-level API + compute_parameter_jacobian!
└─ No → Want to optimize parameters?
    ├─ Yes → Use high-level API + solve_power_flow
    └─ No → Just solving power flow?
        └─ Use either (high-level is simpler)

Example Workflows

Workflow 1: Compute Parameter Jacobian (Low-Level)

# Use case: Study sensitivity ∂y/∂p
psys = ParameterizedSystem(sys)
add_parameter!(psys, :PV, :pg, 1:100)
finalize_parameters!(psys)
cache = CachedAutodiffWorkspace(psys.sys)

# Get baseline solution
p = gather_parameters(psys)
scatter_parameters!(psys, p)
ws = SystemResidualWorkspace(Float64, sys)
dae = DAE(Float64, sys)
# ... solve for y ...

# Compute ∂g/∂p
parameter_sparsity_pattern!(psys, cache)
B = Float64.(psys.sparsity_dgdp)
compute_parameter_jacobian!(B, psys, cache, y, p)

# Compute ∂y/∂p = -J^-1 · B (sensitivity)
J = compute_jacobian(sys, y)
dy_dp = -J \ B

Workflow 2: Optimize Parameters (High-Level)

# Use case: Tune parameters to minimize loss
using Optimization, OptimizationOptimJL, Zygote

psys = ParameterizedSystem(sys)
add_parameter!(psys, :PV, :pg, 1:100)
finalize_parameters!(psys)

# Define objective (pure function)
function objective(p, _)
    y = solve_power_flow(psys, p)
    v = get_bus_voltages(psys.sys, y)
    return sum((v .- 1.0).^2)
end

# Optimize (gradient via Zygote automatically)
p0 = gather_parameters(psys)
prob = OptimizationProblem(objective, p0)
sol = solve(prob, BFGS())  # Uses rrule internally!

println("Optimal parameters: ", sol.u)

Workflow 3: Mixed (Advanced)

# Use case: Custom optimization with manual Jacobian computation

# Pre-compute sparsity (low-level, once)
parameter_sparsity_pattern!(psys, cache)

# Optimization loop
for iter in 1:max_iters
    # High-level: Solve
    y = solve_power_flow(psys, p)

    # Low-level: Custom gradient computation
    B = Float64.(psys.sparsity_dgdp)
    compute_parameter_jacobian!(B, psys, cache, y, p)

    # Custom update rule
    p -= learning_rate * custom_gradient(B, y)
end

Design Principles Followed

1. Separation of Concerns

  • Low-level: How (explicit control)
  • High-level: What (declarative intent)

2. Progressive Disclosure

  • Beginners use solve_power_flow(psys, p)
  • Experts use low-level API when needed

3. Zero-Cost Abstraction

  • High-level compiles to same code as manual
  • rrule is as efficient as hand-coded adjoint

4. Composability

  • High-level functions compose with Julia ecosystem
  • Works with Optimization.jl, Flux.jl, etc.

5. Type Stability

  • Both APIs fully type-stable
  • Compiler can optimize aggressively

Alternative Considered: Unified API with Mode Detection

Idea: Single API that detects AD context

# Automatically works for both modes
y = solve_power_flow(psys, p)

How it works:

  • Check if p contains Dual numbers → forward mode
  • Check if called from Zygote → reverse mode
  • Otherwise → Float64

Rejected because:

  • ❌ Magical behavior (hard to understand)
  • ❌ Can't manually choose mode
  • ❌ Debugging difficulty
  • ❌ Performance unpredictability

Our dual API is better:

  • ✅ Explicit when needed
  • ✅ Simple for common case
  • ✅ Full control when required

Long-Term Vision

  • Keep low-level API for Jacobian computation
  • Document both clearly

    • optimal_power_flow(psys, p)

  • Each with rrule for composability

Long-term

  • Integrate with DifferentialEquations.jl (DAE solve with AD)
  • GPU support for both APIs
  • Symbolic + numeric AD fusion

Summary

Recommended API:

# LOW-LEVEL: Direct control, forward-mode, debugging
scatter_parameters!(psys, p)
evaluate_system_residuals!(ws, dae)
compute_parameter_jacobian!(B, psys, cache, y, p)

# HIGH-LEVEL: Pure functions, reverse-mode, optimization
y = solve_power_flow(psys, p)  # Has rrule
loss = objective(y)
grad = Zygote.gradient(p -> objective(solve_power_flow(psys, p)), p)

Key insight: Different tools for different jobs. Both use the same foundation.

User mental model:

  • "I want to compute a Jacobian" → Low-level API
  • "I want to optimize something" → High-level API
  • "I need custom AD" → Mix both!

This design gives users power (low-level) and simplicity (high-level) simultaneously.
